metadata.description: Users can see the name of the currently running workflow in the control bar, providing immediate context about what is executing
Users can stop the running workflow from the control bar, immediately terminating the AI session, GUI automation, or flow execution as appropriate
Users can see the current execution phase (setup, verification, agentic, or completion) as a badge, understanding where the workflow is in its lifecycle
Users can pause and resume workflow execution (for GUI automation and flow execution types) to temporarily halt activity without losing progress
Users can view the live AI conversation output showing what the AI is thinking, what tools it is calling, and what code changes it is making in real time
Users can see verification results showing whether the AI's changes passed or failed the defined verification steps, with per-step status indicators
Users can click on any summary widget to promote it to the active (large) position, allowing focus on whichever activity stream is most relevant at the moment
Users can switch between widgets using Ctrl+1 through Ctrl+8 keyboard shortcuts for rapid navigation without mouse interaction
The bottom bar provides persistent status information including the active activity type, whether the workflow is running, and elapsed time since the task started
Users can see which orchestrator agent is currently active, understanding the internal execution context of the workflow engine
For iterative workflows, users can see the current iteration count relative to the maximum, understanding how many fix-verify cycles have occurred and how many remain
When multiple workflows are running simultaneously, users can switch between them to monitor each run's progress independently without losing context on any run
Users can navigate to start a new concurrent run from the active runs bar without having to manually navigate away from the dashboard
Each concurrent run displays its own independent execution state including task name, phase, and widget content, so switching between runs shows accurate per-run information
When a workflow finishes, users see a completion summary overlay with the final pass/fail status, providing immediate feedback on whether the automation succeeded
The completion summary shows step-level statistics including counts of successful, failed, and pending steps along with an overall success rate, helping users evaluate the quality of the run
Users can dismiss the completion overlay to return to the dashboard view, or choose to navigate to the Recap page for detailed analysis of the completed run
When a workflow pauses for human review, an approval dialog overlays the dashboard presenting the pending decision to the user without navigating away from the monitoring view
Users can approve or reject the pending workflow action, and upon resolution the workflow automatically resumes execution with the user's decision applied
The approval dialog provides sufficient context about what the AI wants to do so the user can make an informed approval or rejection decision
Users can start an interaction recording session by clicking a prominently displayed Start Recording button, which begins capturing mouse, keyboard, and video data simultaneously
Users see indicators for the three captured input types -- Mouse, Keyboard, and Video -- so they understand the scope of data being recorded
Users see a clear header identifying this as the Interaction Recording tool, with a subtitle explaining it captures input for State Machine creation
Users see explanatory text describing the purpose of recording interactions -- to create State Machines from complex workflows, drags, and multi-step processes
Users can open and close a settings panel to configure recording parameters before starting a session, keeping the main interface uncluttered
Users can adjust the video capture frame rate using an FPS slider, balancing between smoother video quality and smaller file sizes
Users see guidance that higher FPS gives smoother video but larger files, with 30 FPS recommended as the default, helping them make informed configuration choices
The info section explains the purpose (State Machine creation), output format (JSONL events with timestamps), and use cases (drag operations, multi-step workflows, desktop app automation)
Users understand that recordings produce input events in JSONL format with timestamps that can be correlated with video frames for analysis
Users see documented use cases for recordings including complex drag operations, multi-step workflows, and desktop app automation, helping them understand when to use this tool
Users see the Checks page title identifying this as the check builder, within the standard library builder layout
Users can create a new check by clicking a create button, which clears the editor and presents a blank form with sensible defaults for the selected check type
Users can search through saved checks by name to quickly locate a specific check without scrolling through the full list
Each check in the list displays a color-coded type badge (linter, formatter, type checker, test runner, security, build, custom) for quick visual identification
Users can select from multiple check types (linter, formatter, type checker, test runner, security, build, custom), each with appropriate tool options and sensible defaults
Users can configure the shell command that the check executes, with auto-populated defaults based on the selected type and tool (e.g., 'npx eslint . --ext .ts,.tsx' for ESLint)
Users can toggle behavioral flags including auto-fix (attempt fixes before reporting), fail-on-warning (treat warnings as errors), and is-critical (blocking check) to control check execution behavior
Users can save the current check configuration to the library, making it available for use in check groups and workflow verification steps
Users can add tags to checks for organization and discovery, making checks easier to find in the library dashboard and when selecting verification steps in the workflow builder
Users can specify a working directory for check execution, ensuring commands run in the correct project context regardless of the runner's current directory
Users can set a timeout for check execution in seconds, preventing long-running or hung checks from blocking workflow progress indefinitely
Users can delete checks they no longer need, removing them from the library and any check groups that reference them
Users see the Check Groups page title within the standard library builder layout, identifying this as the check group management interface
Users can create a new check group, which opens a blank editor ready for naming, configuring execution mode, and adding checks from the library
Users can search through saved check groups by name to quickly locate a specific group for editing
Users can add individual checks from the library to the group, building up a comprehensive verification suite from reusable check components
Users can remove checks from the group that are no longer needed, refining the verification suite to include only relevant validations
The check selector displays check names and type information so users can identify and select the correct checks for their verification needs
Users can save the check group configuration, making it available as a single verification unit in workflow builder step pickers
Users can choose between sequential and parallel execution modes, controlling whether checks run one at a time or concurrently for faster verification
Users can enable or disable stop-on-failure behavior, choosing between halting at the first failing check for early detection or running all checks for comprehensive results
Users can set a descriptive name and optional description for the check group to identify its purpose when selecting it in workflow builders
Users can add tags to check groups for organization and discovery across the library dashboard
Users can identify the Finding Categories configuration page with a clear heading and subtitle explaining that this controls how findings are categorized and displayed across the application
Users can see all configured categories displayed in a list with their names, colored icons, descriptions, action type labels, and indicators showing whether each category is built-in or custom
Users can reorder categories using up and down controls to define the display sequence in which findings categories appear throughout the application

Users can see a live preview of how a new or edited category will appear before committing changes, including the selected icon rendered in the chosen color
Users can set the default action type for a category, choosing from Auto Fix, Needs Input, Manual, or Informational, to define how the system should handle findings in that category by default
Users can delete custom categories that are no longer needed, with a confirmation dialog warning that findings using the deleted category will become uncategorized

value.textContent: Hidden categories are not shown in reports

metadata.description: Users can toggle individual categories between visible and hidden states, controlling which categories appear in findings reports without permanently deleting them
Users can reset all categories to the default configuration, removing custom categories and restoring built-in ordering, with a confirmation prompt to prevent accidental data loss

value.textContent: Built-in categories cannot be edited or deleted

metadata.description: Users are informed that built-in categories cannot be edited or deleted through clear visual indicators (lock icon and label), preventing confusion about why certain categories lack edit controls
Users can identify the Lifecycle Hooks page with a clear heading and subtitle explaining that hooks are actions configured to run at specific execution events

value.textContent: Configure actions to run at specific execution events

metadata.description: Users understand the purpose of hooks through a descriptive subtitle that explains they configure actions to run at execution events, providing context for users encountering this feature for the first time
When no hooks are configured, users see a helpful empty state with a clear call-to-action to create their first hook, explaining the value of lifecycle hooks rather than showing a blank list
Users can create new lifecycle hooks by clicking a New Hook button, which opens an editor where they can configure the hook's name, URL, event triggers, headers, and payload format
Users can edit existing hooks by clicking an edit action on a hook card, which opens the editor pre-populated with the hook's current configuration for modification
Users can delete hooks they no longer need, with a confirmation dialog that clearly states the action is irreversible and shows the hook name being deleted
Users can test individual hooks to verify connectivity and correct configuration, receiving a result that shows whether the test passed or failed along with the response and duration in milliseconds

When hook operations fail, users see clear error messages with enough detail to diagnose the issue, and can dismiss errors after reading them
Users can identify the UI Bridge integration page with a clear heading and an integration badge, understanding it as the central hub for connecting external applications to the runner
Users can access the Discovery tab to scan for and find UI Bridge-enabled applications running on the local network or at known URLs

Users can access the Source Integration tab to get instructions and tools for permanently integrating the UI Bridge SDK into an application's source code

The page displays an integration badge indicating this is a specialized configuration area for UI Bridge setup and monitoring, distinct from general application settings

Users have access to all five integration tabs (Discovery, Runtime Injection, Source Integration, Health Monitor, State Explorer) covering the complete lifecycle from finding apps to monitoring their ongoing health
Users can freely switch between all five tabs to access different phases of the UI Bridge integration workflow, with each tab retaining its state when the user navigates away and returns
The currently active tab is visually distinguished with a highlighted border or background so users always know which integration phase they are viewing
Users can create new context configurations that define background knowledge and instructions for AI-driven workflow steps
Users can save contexts to the library and reuse them across multiple workflows, ensuring consistent AI behavior
Users can browse all saved contexts in a searchable list and select any context for editing or review
Users can set a descriptive name for each context that identifies its purpose when selecting contexts for workflows
Users can write detailed context content including domain knowledge, coding standards, project conventions, and behavioral constraints for the AI
Users can delete contexts that are no longer needed, removing them from the library permanently

When a context is updated, all workflows referencing it automatically use the updated content on their next execution
While debug settings are loading, users see a 'Loading settings...' status message centered in the page area, indicating the backend is being queried
The loading status element has data-content-role='status' and data-content-label='loading settings' for programmatic detection by automation tools
Users see the section title 'Advanced' at the top of the page, establishing context that these are developer/debugging options
Below the title, users see a description explaining these are 'Developer and debugging options for troubleshooting automation issues'
A wrench icon is displayed next to the title, visually indicating this is a tools/configuration section
When a settings load or save operation fails, an error banner appears with the error message so users understand what went wrong
After a successful save, a success banner appears with 'Settings saved successfully!' message and a checkmark icon, confirming the operation
The success banner automatically disappears after 3 seconds without user interaction
Users see a 'Debug' sub-heading within the settings card, grouping the image-match diagnostic options
The debug settings are wrapped in a rounded card container with subtle background, visually grouping all debug controls together
Users see 'Enable Image Match Debug Mode' as the toggle label, clearly indicating what the setting controls

value.textContent: Collect and display detailed match information

metadata.description: Below the toggle label, users see a description explaining that it collects and displays detailed match information including top match candidates, confidence scores, and failure diagnostics

Users see 'Top Matches to Display' as the label for the slider control
A description explains the slider controls 'Number of top match candidates to show in debug information (1-10)'
The range slider has min=1 and max=10, ensuring users can only select values within the valid range
A number input next to the slider shows the current value and stays synchronized with the slider position. Users can type a value directly
The default value for top matches is 5 when no saved settings exist
Users see a note explaining 'Debug settings take effect on the next image recognition attempt', informing them that changes are not retroactive
The note references the 'Image Recognition Debug tab' where debug output will appear
The note has a 'Note:' label in bold/foreground color followed by muted description text, and is displayed in a subtle primary-tinted background container
Users see a 'Save Debug Settings' button with a settings icon, positioned at the bottom right of the debug section
While a save operation is in progress, the save button is disabled and shows 'Saving...' with a spinner animation, preventing double-submission
After a successful save, the button briefly shows 'Saved!' with a checkmark icon before reverting to the default state
Clicking save calls the Tauri IPC command 'set_debug_settings' with the current enable_image_debug and top_matches_count values
Users see a 'Device Information' heading with a monitor icon, identifying this as the system info section
A description tells users this information is 'useful for debugging and support' and that they can 'Click to copy values'

Users see a 'Device ID' label above the device ID value

Users see a 'Device Name' label above the device name value

Users see a 'Platform' label above the platform value

Clicking the Platform row copies the platform value to clipboard with checkmark feedback
While device info is loading, users see 'Loading device info...' with a spinning refresh icon

When device info fails to load, users see an italic 'Unable to load device information.' message
The unavailable message has data-content-role='status' and data-content-label='device info unavailable' for automation tools

On component mount, the page calls 'get_device_info' to load device identification from the Rust backend

The page content flows vertically with consistent spacing: section header, then debug settings card, then device information card

Users can identify they are on the Error Monitor page and see a heading that clearly communicates the purpose of this view as centralized error tracking
Users can see at-a-glance severity breakdown badges showing how many critical, error, and warning level issues exist, allowing them to immediately gauge the urgency of unresolved problems

Users can expand individual error entries to reveal full error details including the complete message, stack trace, context lines, and resolution notes, providing the information needed to diagnose the root cause
Users can mark new errors as acknowledged to signal that someone is aware of the issue and it does not need further immediate attention from the team

Users can identify which log source produced each error, allowing them to trace issues back to specific applications or services being monitored
Users can see the total count of displayed errors and whether filters are narrowing the view, providing orientation about what portion of the error landscape they are currently examining
Users can search the workflow library by name or description to quickly find specific workflows without scrolling through the full list
Users can filter workflows by category to see only relevant workflow types (e.g., demo, custom, generated)
Users can collapse and expand the workflow library panel to maximize screen space for the execution queue when workflow selection is complete
Users can refresh the workflow library to pick up newly created or modified workflows without navigating away from the page

Multiple states are active simultaneously. The visible screen is described as a set of active states SΞ. A screenshot captures the current screen, which contains elements from multiple co-active states (e.g., a toolbar state, a sidebar state, and a content state all active at once). The same state can be active across many different screens — this is why the same elements appear on multiple pages without belonging to multiple states. States can transition independently without affecting other active states.

An image/element belongs to exactly one state. Images do not cross state boundaries. If the same visual element appears on multiple screens, it is because the state that owns it is active on all those screens. The element is not shared across states — it has one owner. This is a fundamental invariant of the model.

States are defined through co-occurrence analysis. Elements that always appear together form a state. States are the minimal co-occurring sets derived from observing which elements appear on which screens. Example: images 1,2,3 appear on screens A and B; images 1,2,3,4,5 appear on screens C, D, and E. This produces two states: State 1 owns images 1,2,3 (they co-occur on all 5 screens), State 2 owns images 4,5 (they co-occur only on screens C,D,E). A state is formally a collection of related GUI elements chosen to model a distinct configuration of the user interface.

Images signal a state's presence, not its absence. Individual images can reliably confirm a state is active, but a missing image does NOT prove the state is inactive. A state is only deactivated by an explicit transition, never by image disappearance. When a state is active, a specific action performed on one of its objects should give the same expected result every time.

A screenshot contains elements from whichever states were active at capture time. The elementBoundsJson for a screenshot must contain ONLY the elements that were actually visible on screen when the screenshot was taken. These elements may belong to multiple different co-active states — that is expected. But elements from a page that was NOT being viewed must NOT appear in the screenshot's element data.

A screenshot is associated with a state if the state's elements are visible in it. Using the co-occurrence example: State 1 (images 1,2,3) is associated with screenshots from screens A,B,C,D,E. State 2 (images 4,5) is associated with screenshots from screens C,D,E only. A single screenshot will typically match multiple co-active states. A state whose elements were never visible in a screenshot should not match that screenshot.

Element bounding boxes must be actual pixel positions in their specific screenshot. A bounding box records where the element physically appeared at that specific moment. Averaged positions from co-occurrence statistics or estimated positions from relative viewport percentages are not valid bounding box data for a specific screenshot.

When a state opens and obscures another (e.g., a modal dialog over the main window), the covered state is registered as hidden but remains active. The multistate model defines an occlusion function ω: S × S × ℝ → [0,1] that models state visibility. Occlusion is transitive: if s1 occludes s2 and s2 occludes s3, then s1 occludes s3. Blocking states (is_blocking=true) represent modal-like states that prevent interaction with occluded states.

Transitions follow a phased execution model: VALIDATE → OUTGOING → ACTIVATE → INCOMING → EXIT. Activation is a pure memory operation that cannot fail (infallible). If incoming verification fails, the system rolls back to the original state and skips the exit phase. Transitions can activate multiple states atomically and exit multiple states atomically. Each activated state becomes a potential path node for future navigation.
